newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street Journal forced to change section name.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street Journal forced to change section name.

text.p: A California appeals court on Tuesday turned down The Wall Street Journal's request to stay a lower court order temporarily forbidding it from calling a regional weekly section "California Journal."

The ruling means that the section of California business news that appears in state editions of The Wall Street Journal on Wednesdays will have to appear under a different name, at least for this week.

The Wall Street Journal launched the "California Journal" section on Oct. 2. But a Sacramento-based monthly magazine of state politics by the same name, founded in 1970, sued Dow Jones & Co Inc, publishers of the business daily, to stop it from using the name.

California Superior Court Judge Earl Warren Jr. issued a preliminary injunction last week barring The Wall Street Journal from using the name "California Journal" although it said it could publish under another name.
Dow Jones & Co asked a state appeals court in Sacramento to stay Warren's order pending an appeal.
But the court turned down the request for the stay Tuesday, said Rex Heinke, an attorney for Dow Jones.

Dow Jones spokesman Lawrence Budgar said the newspaper would publish the California section Wednesday under a different name. "We are publishing the pages in tomorrow's journal. We will not use the 'California Journal' title and we are considering our other legal options at this point," he said.
Heinke said Dow Jones now planned to ask the California Supreme Court to stay the preliminary order. He said he believed the section would appear Wednesday simply with the heading "California."
Unless overturned or stayed, the preliminary injunction would prevent The Wall Street Journal from using the title until a trial is held to decide the issue permanently.
Jud Clark, president of Information for Public Affairs Inc, which owns "California Journal," said the company was very pleased with the appeals court ruling.
"California Journal" has a circulation of 15,000 compared with The Wall Street Journal's 1.9 million.
